claim: Sensitive genetically-encoded fluorescent glutamate reporters operating with a range of affinities and emission wavelengths are available.
source: Sensitive genetically-encoded fluorescent glutamate reporters operating with a range of affinities and emission wavelengths are available.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the current state of glutamate reporter technology in the field.

claim: Without targeting to synapses, the specificity of the fluorescent signal from glutamate reporters is uncertain, compared to sensors directed at vesicles or other synaptic markers.
source: However, without targeting to synapses, the specificity of the fluorescent signal is uncertain, compared to sensors directed at vesicles or other synaptic markers.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the understanding that non-targeted sensors may report signals from multiple sources.

claim: Chimeras of Stargazin and gamma-8 named SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 were enriched at synapses.
source: Chimeras of Stargazin and gamma-8 that we named SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8, were enriched at synapses, retained function and reported spontaneous glutamate release in rat hippocampal cells, with apparently diffraction-limited spatial precision.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing enrichment at PSD95-positive sites (Figure 3).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 retained function and reported spontaneous glutamate release in rat hippocampal cells.
source: Chimeras of Stargazin and gamma-8 that we named SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8, were enriched at synapses, retained function and reported spontaneous glutamate release in rat hippocampal cells, with apparently diffraction-limited spatial precision.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing spontaneous responses (Figure 2).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 reported spontaneous glutamate release with apparently diffraction-limited spatial precision.
source: Chimeras of Stargazin and gamma-8 that we named SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8, were enriched at synapses, retained function and reported spontaneous glutamate release in rat hippocampal cells, with apparently diffraction-limited spatial precision.
evidence: This is supported by measurements showing half-widths of responses around 300 nm when averaging across frames (Figure 4).

claim: In autaptic mouse neurons cultured on astrocytic microislands, evoked neurotransmitter release could be quantitatively detected at tens of synapses in a field of view whilst evoked currents were recorded simultaneously.
source: In autaptic mouse neurons cultured on astrocytic microislands, evoked neurotransmitter release could be quantitatively detected at tens of synapses in a field of view whilst evoked currents were recorded simultaneously.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous electrophysiology and fluorescence imaging experiments (Figures 6-9).

claim: Stargazin overexpression results in a specific postsynaptic deficit, producing synapses with normal neurotransmitter release but without postsynaptic responses.
source: These experiments revealed a specific postsynaptic deficit from Stargazin overexpression, resulting in synapses with normal neurotransmitter release but without postsynaptic responses.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced EPSCs with early infection but normal fluorescence responses (Figure 5).

claim: The postsynaptic deficit from Stargazin overexpression was reverted by delaying overexpression.
source: This defect was reverted by delaying overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that infection at DIV 6 instead of DIV 3 resulted in more cells with appreciable evoked responses (Figure 5C).

claim: SnFR-γ2 is a linear reporter of the global quantal parameters and short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: By working at different calcium concentrations, we determined that SnFR-γ2 is a linear reporter of the global quantal parameters and short-term synaptic plasticity, whereas iGluSnFR is not.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing excellent correlation between SnFR-γ2 depression and postsynaptic current depression (Figure 8C).

claim: iGluSnFR is not a linear reporter of the global quantal parameters and short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: By working at different calcium concentrations, we determined that SnFR-γ2 is a linear reporter of the global quantal parameters and short-term synaptic plasticity, whereas iGluSnFR is not.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of correlation between iGluSnFR depression and postsynaptic current depression (Figure 8C).

claim: On average, half of iGluSnFR regions of interest (ROIs) showing evoked fluorescence changes had intense rundown.
source: On average, half of iGluSnFR regions of interest (ROIs) showing evoked fluorescence changes had intense rundown, whereas less than 5% of SnFR-γ2 ROIs did.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of peak responses over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Less than 5% of SnFR-γ2 ROIs showed intense rundown.
source: On average, half of iGluSnFR regions of interest (ROIs) showing evoked fluorescence changes had intense rundown, whereas less than 5% of SnFR-γ2 ROIs did.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of peak responses over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Y230F mutation in iGluSnFR increased ∆F/F, the fractional fluorescence change upon glutamate binding.
source: This mutation increased ∆F/F, the fractional fluorescence change upon glutamate binding (possibly by reducing fluorescence in the absence of glutamate), and sped the kinetics of the off-response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data comparing iGluSnFR and Y230F variant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Y230F mutation sped the kinetics of the off-response.
source: This mutation increased ∆F/F, the fractional fluorescence change upon glutamate binding (possibly by reducing fluorescence in the absence of glutamate), and sped the kinetics of the off-response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data showing faster decay time constants for Y230F (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Y230F mutation reduced the apparent affinity for glutamate.
source: As expected, the Y230F mutation also reduced the apparent affinity for glutamate.
evidence: This is an expected consequence of removing a hydroxyl group that coordinates glutamate in the Glt1 domain, supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data.

claim: The Y230F mutant gave almost no fluorescent response in autaptic hippocampal neurons following stimulation.
source: However, we were surprised to discover that the Y230F mutant gave almost no fluorescent response in autaptic hippocampal neurons following stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), whereas in the same cultures, the regular iGluSnFR gave robust fluorescent responses, phase-locked to the postsynaptic currents, as did Synaptophluorin (with about 100× slower off kinetics).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data from autaptic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Regular iGluSnFR gave robust fluorescent responses in autaptic neurons, phase-locked to the postsynaptic currents.
source: However, we were surprised to discover that the Y230F mutant gave almost no fluorescent response in autaptic hippocampal neurons following stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), whereas in the same cultures, the regular iGluSnFR gave robust fluorescent responses, phase-locked to the postsynaptic currents, as did Synaptophluorin (with about 100× slower off kinetics).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data from autaptic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Synaptophluorin gave robust fluorescent responses in autaptic neurons with about 100× slower off kinetics than iGluSnFR.
source: However, we were surprised to discover that the Y230F mutant gave almost no fluorescent response in autaptic hippocampal neurons following stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), whereas in the same cultures, the regular iGluSnFR gave robust fluorescent responses, phase-locked to the postsynaptic currents, as did Synaptophluorin (with about 100× slower off kinetics).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data from autaptic neurons showing slow return to baseline for Synaptophluorin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The Y230F mutant was expressed on the neuronal surface and responded robustly to 10 mM glutamate perfusion over the autaptic neuron.
source: Paradoxically, the Y230F was expressed on the neuronal surface and responded robustly to 10 mM glutamate perfusion over the autaptic neuron (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing responses to direct glutamate application (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The fluorescence from unmodified iGluSnFR on average occurs over a spatial extent much larger than an individual synapse (~10 µm2).
source: Combined with the observation that the fluorescence from unmodified iGluSnFR on average occurs over a spatial extent much larger than an individual synapse (~10 µm2, see below) this observation led us to hypothesise that the low-affinity sensor was on average not sufficiently close to the synaptic glutamate signal to properly report it.
evidence: This is supported by ROI size analysis showing larger areas for iGluSnFR compared to SnFR-γ2 (Figure 7).

claim: The low-affinity sensor was on average not sufficiently close to the synaptic glutamate signal to properly report it.
source: Combined with the observation that the fluorescence from unmodified iGluSnFR on average occurs over a spatial extent much larger than an individual synapse (~10 µm2, see below) this observation led us to hypothesise that the low-affinity sensor was on average not sufficiently close to the synaptic glutamate signal to properly report it.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Y230F failed to respond to evoked release despite responding to direct glutamate application.

claim: Inline fusion of iGluSnFR at a permissive site in AMPA receptor subunits GluA1 and GluA2 extracellular region produced a sensor with a very small ∆F/F.
source: Inline fusion at a permissive site in AMPA receptor subunits GluA1 and GluA2 extracellular region produced a sensor with a very small ∆F/F (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data showing weak fluorescence responses for GluA2/A1 SnFR chimeras (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 had similar performance to the original iGluSnFR in HEK cells.
source: These chimeric sensors had similar performance to the original iGluSnFR and associated normally with AMPA receptor complexes in HEK cells (Figure 1), also acting to modulate AMPA receptor gating.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data showing similar fluorescence responses and kinetics (Figure 1).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 associated normally with AMPA receptor complexes in HEK cells.
source: These chimeric sensors had similar performance to the original iGluSnFR and associated normally with AMPA receptor complexes in HEK cells (Figure 1), also acting to modulate AMPA receptor gating.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing modulation of AMPA receptor currents (Figure 1F, G).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 act to modulate AMPA receptor gating.
source: These chimeric sensors had similar performance to the original iGluSnFR and associated normally with AMPA receptor complexes in HEK cells (Figure 1), also acting to modulate AMPA receptor gating.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing changes in steady-state currents and I-V relations (Figure 1F, G).

claim: The two reporters (SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8) had similar apparent affinity for glutamate (within a factor of 2) to iGluSnFR.
source: The two reporters had similar apparent affinity for glutamate (within a factor of 2) to iGluSnFR, quite distinct from published 'low-affinity' variants (Helassa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by glutamate concentration-response relationships measured in HEK cells (Figure 1C).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 have quite distinct affinity from published 'low-affinity' variants.
source: The two reporters had similar apparent affinity for glutamate (within a factor of 2) to iGluSnFR, quite distinct from published 'low-affinity' variants (Helassa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published work on low-affinity iGluSnFR variants.

claim: Bulk rat hippocampal cultures infected with the AAV of iGluSnFR gave wide, diffuse and relatively infrequent fluorescent signals.
source: Bulk rat hippocampal cultures infected with the AAV of iGluSnFR gave wide, diffuse and, in our hands, relatively infrequent fluorescent signals (see Figure 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data from bulk cultures (Figure 2, Video 1).

claim: Hippocampal bulk cultures infected with SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 viruses revealed regular fluorescence spikes (typically about 1 Hz frequency).
source: Hippocampal bulk cultures infected with these viruses revealed regular fluorescence spikes (typically about 1 Hz frequency, see Figure 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data from bulk cultures (Figure 2, Video 2).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 showed a more localised signal at hand-picked regions of interest (ROIs) compared to iGluSnFR.
source: At hand-picked regions of interest (ROIs), SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 showed a more localised signal (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing distinct signals at ROIs with minimal signal at adjacent regions (Figure 2).

claim: About 50% greater average intensity in PSD spots was detected for SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 compared to iGluSnFR.
source: We detected about 50% greater average intensity in PSD spots for SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 (p = 0.03 and 0.06, respectively), as compared to iGluSnFR, suggesting that SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 are weakly enriched at synapses and probably exchange with extrasynaptic sites.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data quantifying surface GFP intensity in PSD95 puncta (Figure 3B).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 are weakly enriched at synapses and probably exchange with extrasynaptic sites.
source: We detected about 50% greater average intensity in PSD spots for SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 (p = 0.03 and 0.06, respectively), as compared to iGluSnFR, suggesting that SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 are weakly enriched at synapses and probably exchange with extrasynaptic sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modest enrichment observed in immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The PSD size was slightly reduced for SnFR-γ2 compared to iGluSnFR.
source: The PSD size was slightly reduced for SnFR-γ2 compared to iGluSnFR, but the number of PSD spots per neuron imaged was similar across all conditions.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data quantifying mean area of PSD95 puncta (Figure 3C).

claim: The number of PSD spots per neuron imaged was similar across all conditions (iGluSnFR, SnFR-γ2, SnFR-γ8).
source: The PSD size was slightly reduced for SnFR-γ2 compared to iGluSnFR, but the number of PSD spots per neuron imaged was similar across all conditions.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data quantifying number of PSD95 puncta per field of view (Figure 3D).

claim: Responsive SnFR-γ2 spots were enriched at Homer positive spots, presumably corresponding to synaptic connections.
source: Consistent with our results from immunocytochemistry (Figure 3), responsive SnFR-γ2 spots were enriched at Homer positive spots, presumably corresponding to synaptic connections (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-infection experiments with Homer-tdTomato showing colocalization (Figure 4A).

claim: Background-subtracted heat maps revealed a sharper signal for SnFR-γ2 compared to iGluSnFR.
source: Background-subtracted heat maps revealed a sharper signal for SnFR-γ2 compared to iGluSnFR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by heat map analysis of spontaneous fluorescence signals (Figure 4B).

claim: The apparent half-width of the responses during spontaneous neurotransmission was on average less than 500 nm for SnFR-γ2, or about three-fold narrower than for iGluSnFR.
source: Taking a line profile through the centre of the peak response showed that the apparent half-width of the responses during spontaneous neurotransmission was on average less than 500 nm (Figure 4D, E) or about three-fold narrower than for iGluSnFR in our cultures.
evidence: This is supported by line profile analysis and Gaussian fitting of fluorescence responses (Figure 4D, E).

claim: When averaging across frames, the half-width at some sites was of the order of 300 nm, or probably limited by diffraction of the microscope.
source: When averaging across frames, the half-width at some sites was of the order of 300 nm, or in other words, probably limited by diffraction of the microscope (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by line profile analysis showing widths approaching the diffraction limit (Figure 4D).

claim: Mean amplitudes from both the peak and subsequent two frames from SnFR-γ2 were slightly increased compared to iGluSnFR for spontaneous neurotransmission.
source: For this spontaneous neurotransmission, mean amplitudes from both the peak and subsequent two frames from SnFR-γ2 were slightly increased compared to iGluSnFR (Figure 4F, G), possibly because SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 experienced a higher degree of saturation than their non-targeted version (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of peak and averaged fluorescence changes (Figure 4F, G).

claim: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 possibly experienced a higher degree of saturation than their non-targeted version.
source: For this spontaneous neurotransmission, mean amplitudes from both the peak and subsequent two frames from SnFR-γ2 were slightly increased compared to iGluSnFR (Figure 4F, G), possibly because SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 experienced a higher degree of saturation than their non-targeted version (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed increase in normalized fluorescence changes.

claim: The normalised peak fluorescence of the SnFR-γ2 response was greater than that for iGluSnFR.
source: The normalised peak fluorescence of the SnFR-γ2 response was also greater than that for iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of peak normalized fluorescence changes (Figure 4F).

claim: About half the autaptic neurons showed a near absence of evoked neurotransmission following infection with SnFR-γ2 or SnFR-γ8 before DIV 3.
source: Although not obviously related, we also regularly measured a near absence of evoked neurotransmission (Figure 5B) in about half the autaptic neurons following infection before DIV 3.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced or absent EPSCs in many cells (Figure 5B, C).

claim: Robust evoked glutamate release (as reported by fluorescence changes from the sensors) was present in neurons with reduced EPSCs.
source: Robust evoked glutamate release (as reported by fluorescence changes from the sensors) was present, and we failed to detect any change in VGLUT puncta size or number on MAP2-positive neurites in immunostaining experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), when comparing to non-infected neurons or neurons infected with iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing normal fluorescence responses despite absent EPSCs (Figure 5A, B).

claim: No change in VGLUT puncta size or number on MAP2-positive neurites was detected in immunostaining experiments when comparing to non-infected neurons or neurons infected with iGluSnFR.
source: Robust evoked glutamate release (as reported by fluorescence changes from the sensors) was present, and we failed to detect any change in VGLUT puncta size or number on MAP2-positive neurites in immunostaining experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), when comparing to non-infected neurons or neurons infected with iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data quantifying VGLUT puncta (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: A majority of autaptic neurons retained an appreciable evoked response following late infection (after DIV 6).
source: Indeed, a majority of autaptic neurons retained an appreciable evoked response following late infection (neurons giving excitatory postsynaptic current [EPSC] >100 pA: 7 of 31, DIV 3 infection and 24 of 45, DIV 6; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data comparing early and late infection (Figure 5C).

claim: Infection with iGluSnFR does not affect evoked currents much.
source: Given that infection with iGluSnFR does not affect evoked currents much (Figure 5C), we reasoned that auxiliary proteins in overexpression might be causing the postsynaptic deficit.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing normal EPSCs in iGluSnFR-infected neurons (Figure 5C).

claim: Early infection (before DIV 3) of either of two Stg constructs tagged with mScarlet were highly deleterious to evoked currents in autapses.
source: Indeed, early infection (before DIV 3) of either of two Stg constructs tagged with mScarlet (with or without the fused N-terminal NETO transmembrane section) were highly deleterious to evoked currents in autapses (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced EPSCs with early Stargazin overexpression (Figure 5F, G).

claim: Miniature currents were strongly reduced in amplitude and frequency with early Stargazin overexpression.
source: Miniature currents were also strongly reduced in amplitude and frequency, to the point that we failed to detect minis in a large proportion of cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), whereas paired-pulse ratio (20-ms interval) was unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data measuring miniature EPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Paired-pulse ratio (20-ms interval) was unaffected by early Stargazin overexpression.
source: Miniature currents were also strongly reduced in amplitude and frequency, to the point that we failed to detect minis in a large proportion of cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), whereas paired-pulse ratio (20-ms interval) was unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data measuring paired-pulse ratios (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: A late infection (after DIV 6) with Stargazin constructs had much less impact on evoked currents.
source: However, a late infection (after DIV 6) had much less impact, suggesting a previously unheralded developmental pathology at the postsynapse from early Stargazin overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data comparing early and late infection with Stargazin constructs (Figure 5G).

claim: Early Stargazin overexpression causes a previously unheralded developmental pathology at the postsynapse.
source: However, a late infection (after DIV 6) had much less impact, suggesting a previously unheralded developmental pathology at the postsynapse from early Stargazin overexpression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that timing of infection affects the severity of the postsynaptic deficit.

claim: The signal from iGluSnFR in response to evoked transmission at 5 Hz was more diffuse than the response of SnFR-γ2 in autaptic neurons.
source: In autaptic neurons infected with AAVs at DIV 6, the signal from iGluSnFR in response to evoked transmission at 5 Hz was again more diffuse than the response of SnFR-γ2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data comparing iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2 responses (Figure 6).

claim: For most ROIs in the SnFR-γ2 cells, the neighbour region was silent.
source: Whilst neighbour and principal fluorescence time series usually matched well for iGluSnFR (Figure 6C), for most ROIs in the SnFR-γ2 cells, the neighbour region was silent (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence time series from principal and neighbor ROIs (Figure 6F).

claim: The correlation coefficient between fluorescence time series for principal and neighbour ROIs was less for SnFR-γ2 than for iGluSnFR.
source: Correspondingly, the correlation coefficient between fluorescence time series for principal and neighbour ROIs was less for SnFR-γ2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of paired ROI time series (Figure 6).

claim: The ROIs found by automatic scanning were much smaller on average for SnFR-γ2 (mean areas: 2.5 vs. 9.6 μm2) than for iGluSnFR.
source: Strikingly, but perhaps unsurprisingly, the ROIs found in this way (Figure 7) were much smaller on average for SnFR-γ2 (mean areas: 2.5 vs. 9.6 μm2) than for iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is supported by ROI size analysis from automatically detected regions (Figure 7C).

claim: On average, neurons infected with iGluSnFR gave about twice as many ROIs as either SnFR-γ2 or SnFR-γ8.
source: On average, neurons infected with iGluSnFR gave about twice as many ROIs as either SnFR-γ2 or SnFR-γ8 (Figure 7C; 207 ROIs for iGluSnFR, 107 for SnFR-γ2, and 97 for SnFR-γ8, each over 6 neurons).
evidence: This is supported by ROI count analysis from automatically detected regions (Figure 7D).

claim: At least half of automatically identified ROIs from the iGluSnFR movies showed rundown greater than 50%.
source: Indeed at least half of automatically identified ROIs from the iGluSnFR movies showed rundown greater than 50% (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), whereas less than 7% of ROIs selected from SnFR-γ2 cells did.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of peak response changes over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Less than 7% of ROIs selected from SnFR-γ2 cells showed rundown greater than 50%.
source: Indeed at least half of automatically identified ROIs from the iGluSnFR movies showed rundown greater than 50% (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), whereas less than 7% of ROIs selected from SnFR-γ2 cells did.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of peak response changes over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: There was no relation between the size of the compound ROI and the extent of rundown.
source: There was no relation between the size of the compound ROI and the extent of rundown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis showing no correlation between ROI size and rundown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The average baseline fluorescence intensity (F0) was stable during the recordings for both iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2.
source: Moreover, the average baseline fluorescence intensity (F0) was stable during the recordings, and showed little change for either iGluSnFR or SnFR-γ2 in our recording conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of baseline fluorescence over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: The stable baseline fluorescence speaks against photobleaching as a source of the aberrant behaviour of iGluSnFR in some ROIs.
source: This observation speaks against photobleaching as a source of the aberrant behaviour of iGluSnFR in some ROIs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that baseline fluorescence remained stable despite rundown of evoked responses.

claim: The EPSC peak amplitude typically reduced by about 40% over an entire run for both iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2.
source: The EPSC peak amplitude typically reduced by about 40% over an entire run (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2), for both iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of EPSC rundown over 50 episodes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, D).

claim: The iGluSnFR rundown exaggerated the current rundown.
source: Therefore, the iGluSnFR rundown exaggerated the current rundown and the SnFR-γ2 construct perhaps underestimated it, consistent with reporting different sources of glutamate (e.g., iGluSnFR preferentially reporting spillover).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing fluorescence rundown to EPSC rundown.

claim: The SnFR-γ2 construct perhaps underestimated the current rundown.
source: Therefore, the iGluSnFR rundown exaggerated the current rundown and the SnFR-γ2 construct perhaps underestimated it, consistent with reporting different sources of glutamate (e.g., iGluSnFR preferentially reporting spillover).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing fluorescence rundown to EPSC rundown.

claim: iGluSnFR preferentially reports spillover glutamate.
source: Therefore, the iGluSnFR rundown exaggerated the current rundown and the SnFR-γ2 construct perhaps underestimated it, consistent with reporting different sources of glutamate (e.g., iGluSnFR preferentially reporting spillover).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the different rundown behavior of iGluSnFR compared to SnFR-γ2.

claim: Postsynaptic currents in iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2 showed similar short-term plasticity.
source: Postsynaptic currents in iGluSnFR and SnFR-γ2 showed similar short-term plasticity (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing similar depression patterns (Figure 8A, B).

claim: With 2 mM calcium, the peak current amplitude exhibited mild depression during trains of five pulses.
source: With 2 mM calcium, the peak current amplitude exhibited mild depression during trains of five pulses.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing normalized EPSC amplitudes during trains (Figure 8A, B).

claim: The initial amplitude was larger and showed a stronger reduction at 4 mM calcium, consistent with multivesicular release and vesicle depletion.
source: The initial amplitude was larger and showed a stronger reduction at 4 mM calcium, consistent with multivesicular release and vesicle depletion, whereas responses were small and did not change during the train for 0.5 mM calcium.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing calcium-dependent changes in EPSC amplitudes and depression (Figure 8A, B).

claim: Responses were small and did not change during the train for 0.5 mM calcium.
source: The initial amplitude was larger and showed a stronger reduction at 4 mM calcium, consistent with multivesicular release and vesicle depletion, whereas responses were small and did not change during the train for 0.5 mM calcium.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing minimal depression at low calcium (Figure 8A, B).

claim: There was no relation between the depression of the postsynaptic AMPA receptor response during each train and the average depression of the fluorescence signal over the ROIs in movies recorded from iGluSnFR expressing cells.
source: In movies recorded from iGluSnFR expressing cells, there was no relation between the depression of the postsynaptic AMPA receptor response during each train and the average depression of the fluorescence signal over the ROIs (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing no relationship between EPSC and fluorescence depression for iGluSnFR (Figure 8C).

claim: There was an excellent correlation between the SnFR-γ2 depression and the postsynaptic current depression at 2 and 4 mM calcium.
source: In contrast, there was an excellent correlation between the SnFR-γ2 depression and the postsynaptic current depression at 2 and 4 mM calcium (Figure 8C) indicating that the synaptic release reported by SnFR-γ2 across tens of sites per neuron accurately represents the average synaptic response to glutamate release.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationship between EPSC and fluorescence depression for SnFR-γ2 (Figure 8C).

claim: The synaptic release reported by SnFR-γ2 across tens of sites per neuron accurately represents the average synaptic response to glutamate release.
source: In contrast, there was an excellent correlation between the SnFR-γ2 depression and the postsynaptic current depression at 2 and 4 mM calcium (Figure 8C) indicating that the synaptic release reported by SnFR-γ2 across tens of sites per neuron accurately represents the average synaptic response to glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong correlation between fluorescence and electrophysiology measurements.

claim: The lack of correlation of signals from iGluSnFR is likely because of rundown and also possibly because indistinct localisation leads it to report stray glutamate as well as synaptic glutamate.
source: The lack of correlation of signals from iGluSnFR is likely because of rundown and also possibly because indistinct localisation leads it to report stray glutamate as well as synaptic glutamate, particularly in conditions where repeated glutamate release occurs (5 Hz or above, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the poor correlation observed with iGluSnFR.

claim: The higher correlation in fluorescence between neighbouring sites observed for iGluSnFR exemplifies the phenomenon of reporting stray glutamate.
source: The higher correlation in fluorescence between neighbouring sites that we observed for iGluSnFR (Figure 6) exemplifies this phenomenon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that iGluSnFR shows correlated signals at neighboring ROIs.

claim: For SnFR-γ2, the average release probability over all ROIs increased monotonically with Ca2+ concentration in all 6 cells examined.
source: For CV analysis, independent of the choice of N value, the average release probability over all ROIs, estimated from SnFR-γ2, increased monotonically with Ca2+ concentration, as expected from decades of electrophysiological analysis (Figure 8G, 6/6 cells).
evidence: This is supported by CV analysis showing monotonic increase in release probability with calcium for all SnFR-γ2 cells (Figure 8G).

claim: The release probability estimated from iGluSnFR responses only increased monotonically for two out of six cells.
source: By contrast, the release probability estimated from iGluSnFR responses only increased monotonically for two out of six cells (Figure 8G), suggesting it is a poor reporter of synaptic activity in this context.
evidence: This is supported by CV analysis showing non-monotonic changes in release probability with calcium for most iGluSnFR cells (Figure 8G).

claim: iGluSnFR is a poor reporter of synaptic activity in the context of CV analysis.
source: By contrast, the release probability estimated from iGluSnFR responses only increased monotonically for two out of six cells (Figure 8G), suggesting it is a poor reporter of synaptic activity in this context.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that iGluSnFR fails to show expected calcium-dependent changes in release probability.

claim: Previous analysis on connected cultured hippocampal neurons using electrophysiology gave similar values (N = 5 and PR = 0.4 from CV analysis) to the ones obtained from SnFR-γ2 at 2 mM Ca2+.
source: Previous analysis on connected cultured hippocampal neurons using electrophysiology gave similar values (N = 5 and PR = 0.4 from CV analysis Bekkers and Stevens, 1990) to the ones that we obtained from SnFR-γ2 at 2 mM Ca2+.
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published electrophysiological work.

claim: For SnFR-γ2, 80% of the automatically-found ROIs were usable for quantal analysis.
source: For SnFR-γ2, 80% of the automatically-found ROIs were usable for quantal analysis, and these ROIs reported a range of release probabilities similar to those determined from the CV analysis (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of usable ROIs for histogram fitting (Figure 9E).

claim: SnFR-γ2 ROIs reported a range of release probabilities similar to those determined from the CV analysis.
source: For SnFR-γ2, 80% of the automatically-found ROIs were usable for quantal analysis, and these ROIs reported a range of release probabilities similar to those determined from the CV analysis (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of release probabilities from CV analysis and histogram fitting (Figure 9G).

claim: In the majority of ROIs, the binomial model gave a better fit than the Poisson model according to the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.
source: In the majority of ROIs, according to the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test for the goodness of fit, the binomial model gave a better fit than the Poisson model (Bhumbra and Beato, 2013; Malagon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of binomial and Poisson fits to amplitude histograms.

claim: For SnFR-γ2, the distributions of peak amplitudes gave clearer multiple peaks than iGluSnFR responses.
source: For SnFR-γ2, the distributions of peak amplitudes gave clearer multiple peaks (Figure 9C, D) than iGluSnFR responses.
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of amplitude histograms (Figure 9C, D).

claim: The ranges of numbers of components and open probabilities determined from global fitting of individual synapses were slightly narrower for SnFR-γ2 than for iGluSnFR.
source: The ranges of numbers of components and open probabilities determined from global fitting of individual synapses were slightly narrower for SnFR-γ2 than for iGluSnFR (Figure 9F, G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of distributions of N and release probability from histogram fitting (Figure 9F, G).

claim: On average, SnFR-γ2 gave similar quantal parameters from global estimates of the CV to previous electrophysiological work (N = 5 and PR = 0.4 from CV analysis on pairs of cultured rat neurons).
source: On average, SnFR-γ2 also gave similar quantal parameters from global estimates of the CV to previous electrophysiological work (N = 5 and PR = 0.4 from CV analysis on pairs of cultured rat neurons; Bekkers and Stevens, 1990).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published electrophysiological work.

claim: Postsynaptic short-term plasticity (e.g., from desensitisation) is limited enough to be neglected at the frequencies used (up to 5 Hz).
source: These observations suggest that SnFR-γ2 is a fair reporter of presynaptic release, and that postsynaptic short-term plasticity (e.g., from desensitisation) is limited enough to be neglected at the frequencies we used (up to 5 Hz) (Malagon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SnFR-γ2 accurately reports short-term depression as measured by electrophysiology.

claim: Optical report of glutamate concentration signal eliminates postsynaptic receptors as a source of variability.
source: Optical report of glutamate concentration signal eliminates postsynaptic receptors as a source of variability.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the advantage of measuring glutamate directly rather than postsynaptic responses.

claim: Simulations suggest that most variability comes from the variation in glutamate released by each vesicle.
source: Simulations suggest that most variability comes from the variation in glutamate released by each vesicle (Franks et al., 2003), but we saw little evidence for this.
evidence: This is a reference to previous simulation work, contrasted with the current observations.

claim: The authors saw little evidence for variation in glutamate released by each vesicle as a major source of variability.
source: Simulations suggest that most variability comes from the variation in glutamate released by each vesicle (Franks et al., 2003), but we saw little evidence for this.
evidence: This is based on the observation of relatively invariant quantal sizes in the histogram analysis.

claim: SnFR-γ2 is saturated by even poorly loaded vesicles.
source: Perhaps SnFR-γ2 is saturated by even poorly loaded vesicles, but fitting distributions with release sites (N) up to 8 or more, corresponding to up to 8 quanta in high Ca2+, suggests this is not the case.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation that is then argued against based on the fitting results.

claim: AMPA-type glutamate receptors have a lower affinity for glutamate than SnFR-γ2.
source: AMPA-type glutamate receptors have a lower affinity for glutamate than SnFR-γ2, and so the invariant quantal size reported by SnFR-γ2 would in any case translate to less robust AMPA receptor activation.
evidence: This is based on known properties of AMPA receptors and the measured affinity of SnFR-γ2.

claim: Synaptic AMPARs are probably often not saturated due to a steep dependence on geometric factors.
source: Synaptic AMPARs are probably often not saturated due to a steep dependence on geometric factors (Savtchenko and Rusakov, 2014), or because the number of AMPA receptors available is so variable.
evidence: This is based on previous modeling work and general knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claim: Confining iGluSnFR to the presynaptic terminal gives quantal amplitude distributions.
source: In clear contrast, confining iGluSnFR to the presynaptic terminal (in the case that anatomy allows this) gives quantal amplitude distributions (Duerst et al., 2020; Dürst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work showing that presynaptic targeting of iGluSnFR produces clearer quantal distributions.

claim: Changing the calcium concentration and examining the same terminal appears to be beneficial in determining quantal parameters.
source: In particular, we can confirm that changing the calcium concentration and examining the same terminal appears to be beneficial in determining quantal parameters (Duerst et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the current experimental results and comparison to previous work.

claim: Bleaching reduces ∆F/F because a large proportion of the background fluorescence signal comes from either intracellular or occluded sensor molecules.
source: One possibility is that bleaching reduces ∆F/F because a large proportion of the background fluorescence signal comes from either intracellular or occluded sensor molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the rundown phenomenon observed with iGluSnFR.

claim: If bleaching were more intense when glutamate is bound, and iGluSnFR were to have more average occupancy by glutamate than the confined SnFR-γ2, this could specifically reduce ∆F.
source: If bleaching (or another process that eliminates signal, like endocytosis) were more intense when glutamate is bound, and iGluSnFR were to in turn have more average occupancy by glutamate than the confined SnFR-γ2, this could specifically reduce ∆F.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the differential rundown behavior.

claim: SnFR-γ2 would be protected from glutamate exposure by seeing only fast glutamate transients that saturate the sensor and immediately disperse.
source: In such a scheme, SnFR-γ2 would be protected from glutamate exposure by seeing only fast glutamate transients that saturate the sensor and immediately disperse, as opposed to a larger iGluSnFR capacity that is saturated for longer periods by spillover (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation illustrated in a schematic diagram.

claim: The membrane protein without any PSD ligand is not excluded from the PSD, even though the diffusion of any protein is impeded within the PSD.
source: The diffusion within synapses of the same single TM protein with and without a PSD-binding ligand (from the Stg C-terminus) provides an excellent comparison for our purposes (Li and Blanpied, 2016). These studies show that even though the diffusion of any protein is impeded within the PSD, the membrane protein without any PSD ligand is not excluded.
evidence: This is based on previous work studying protein diffusion at synapses.

claim: The results are consistent with the idea that the PDGFR motif of the original iGluSnFR is excluded from synapses.
source: However, our results are consistent with the idea that the PDGFR motif of the original iGluSnFR is excluded from synapses, as corroborated by expansion microscopy (Aggarwal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current results and comparison to recent expansion microscopy work.

claim: The density of SnFR-γ2 must be less outside the synapse than inside, assuming equal expression and the concentration of membrane proteins with a PDZ ligand inside PSDs.
source: Assuming equal expression, and the concentration of membrane proteins with a PDZ ligand inside PSDs (Li and Blanpied, 2016), the density of SnFR-γ2 must be less outside the synapse (also see Figure 6).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relative areas of synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane.

claim: A greater capacity outside the synapse would mean that, even without being excluded from synapses, iGluSnFR is biased against measuring synaptic glutamate.
source: On average, a greater capacity outside the synapse would mean that, even without being excluded from synapses, iGluSnFR is biased against measuring synaptic glutamate.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of non-targeted sensor distribution.

claim: Neither iGluSnFR nor SnFR-γ2 can identify single release events in the experimental conditions used.
source: Neither iGluSnFR nor SnFR-γ2 can identify single release events in our conditions, but for different reasons.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the limitations of both sensors.

claim: The iGluSnFR signal often runs down intensely, meaning that the quantal estimate ∆F changes during a recording and cannot be considered constant across different conditions.
source: The iGluSnFR signal often runs down intensely, meaning that the quantal estimate ∆F changes during a recording and cannot be considered constant across different conditions.
evidence: This is based on the observation of rundown in iGluSnFR ROIs.

claim: SnFR-γ2 cannot reliably report isolated single release events because the amplitude of the signal is too small.
source: SnFR-γ2 cannot reliably report isolated single release events because the amplitude of the signal is too small.
evidence: This is based on the observation of low signal-to-noise ratio for SnFR-γ2 responses.

claim: Spontaneous neurotransmission in cultures (in the absence of TTX) could be readily resolved by SnFR-γ2, at spot-like ROIs.
source: However, spontaneous neurotransmission in cultures (in the absence of TTX) could be readily resolved by SnFR-γ2, at spot-like ROIs.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing spontaneous responses (Figure 2).

claim: The improved spatial profiles of SnFR-γ2 are expected to be beneficial for short-term plasticity studies.
source: For short-term plasticity, whereby synapses are reactivated over 50-ms intervals or similar, the improved spatial profiles of SnFR-γ2 are expected to be beneficial (Helassa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the improved spatial resolution of SnFR-γ2 and comparison to previous work.

claim: Using mouse auxiliary proteins to anchor the glutamate reporter opposite to release sites may not be universal, and may influence synaptic transmission in other systems in undesirable ways.
source: Using mouse auxiliary proteins to anchor the glutamate reporter opposite to release sites may not be universal, and may influence synaptic transmission in other systems in undesirable ways.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: Stargazin overexpression reduced miniature current amplitude and frequency but did not affect paired-pulse response.
source: Stargazin overexpression reduced miniature current amplitude and frequency but did not affect paired-pulse response (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and glutamate release was intact (from SnFR-γ2 signals).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data measuring miniature EPSCs and paired-pulse ratios (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Glutamate release was intact with Stargazin overexpression (from SnFR-γ2 signals).
source: Stargazin overexpression reduced miniature current amplitude and frequency but did not affect paired-pulse response (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and glutamate release was intact (from SnFR-γ2 signals).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing normal SnFR-γ2 responses despite reduced EPSCs.

claim: Stargazin overexpression strongly suggests a postsynaptic deficit in cultured hippocampal cells.
source: This strongly suggests a postsynaptic deficit in cultured hippocampal cells but in other neuronal types, effects might be different.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of effects observed with Stargazin overexpression.

claim: When inadvertent recordings of GABAergic cells were made, there was no response of the iGluSnFR sensors and no obvious effect on evoked inhibitory current magnitudes.
source: When we made inadvertent recordings of GABAergic cells, which we subsequently discarded, we saw no response of the iGluSnFR sensors, but nor was there any obvious effect on evoked inhibitory current magnitudes.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments that were not included in the main analysis.

claim: Sensor performance is always worse in the in vivo context.
source: Notably, sensor performance is always worse in the in vivo context, and our sensor, along with a similar recently reported approach (Aggarwal et al., 2022), is probably better suited to quantitative studies of synaptic transmission in vitro, rather than in vivo work, even though its performance should not be worse than the original iGluSnFR construct.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of sensor performance in different contexts.

claim: The sensor is probably better suited to quantitative studies of synaptic transmission in vitro, rather than in vivo work.
source: Notably, sensor performance is always worse in the in vivo context, and our sensor, along with a similar recently reported approach (Aggarwal et al., 2022), is probably better suited to quantitative studies of synaptic transmission in vitro, rather than in vivo work, even though its performance should not be worse than the original iGluSnFR construct.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the characteristics of the sensor and comparison to iGluSnFR.

claim: Stargazin has a very long first intron.
source: Stargazin has a very long first intron (Letts et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement of known molecular biology of the Stargazin gene.

claim: The long first intron of Stg is the target of three mutations (including the original stargazer mouse) which reduce or abolish γ-2 mRNA.
source: This long first intron of Stg is the target of three mutations (including the original stargazer mouse) which reduce or abolish γ-2 mRNA (Letts et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement of known genetics of Stargazin mutations.

claim: Long introns extend transcription times and are thought to delay expression.
source: Because long introns extend transcription times, they are thought to delay expression.
evidence: This is a statement of general molecular biology knowledge.

claim: Release was apparently normal in neurons with reduced EPSCs following Stargazin overexpression.
source: The most curious aspect of our observations was that release was apparently normal, and presynaptic VGLUT1 markers were not affected.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging and immunocytochemistry data.

claim: Presynaptic VGLUT1 markers were not affected by Stargazin overexpression.
source: The most curious aspect of our observations was that release was apparently normal, and presynaptic VGLUT1 markers were not affected.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Synapses in neurons infected with Stargazin or chimeras on or before DIV 3 were non-functional, despite their otherwise normal appearance.
source: It is not routine to perform electrophysiological characterisation of synapses following molecular interventions before imaging, however, the synapses in neurons infected with Stargazin or chimeras on or before DIV 3 were non-functional, despite their otherwise normal appearance.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing absent or reduced EPSCs despite normal fluorescence and morphology.

claim: Stargazin is not the ideal host for the iGluSnFR sensor domain.
source: It is likely that Stargazin is not the ideal host for the iGluSnFR sensor domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the postsynaptic deficit observed with Stargazin-based constructs.

claim: Auxiliary proteins that are not complexed to AMPA receptors probably fill slots in the postsynaptic density, reducing postsynaptic currents.
source: Auxiliary proteins that are not complexed to AMPA receptors probably fill slots in the postsynaptic density, reducing postsynaptic currents.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the postsynaptic deficit.

claim: The performance of the SnFR-γ8 construct was similar to SnFR-γ2, but neuronal labelling was often less broad, giving fewer ROIs that responded.
source: The performance of the SnFR-γ8 construct was similar to SnFR-γ2, but neuronal labelling was often less broad, giving fewer ROIs that responded.
evidence: This is based on observations from fluorescence imaging experiments.

claim: Tethered sensors preferentially select stronger synapses.
source: It is likely that tethered sensors preferentially select stronger synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation that fewer ROIs are detected with targeted sensors.

claim: The additional transmembrane helix from NETO2 appears to reduce expression.
source: The additional transmembrane helix from NETO2 appears to reduce expression (although this may indeed be desirable) and is quantitatively more damaging to synaptic transmission than Stargazin in a more native form (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on comparison of effects of different Stargazin constructs on EPSCs.

claim: The additional transmembrane helix from NETO2 is quantitatively more damaging to synaptic transmission than Stargazin in a more native form.
source: The additional transmembrane helix from NETO2 appears to reduce expression (although this may indeed be desirable) and is quantitatively more damaging to synaptic transmission than Stargazin in a more native form (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data comparing mS-Stg and mS-N-Stg constructs (Figure 5G).

claim: The targeted sensor did not have distinctly better fluorescence performance in terms of signal to noise compared to iGluSnFR.
source: Our targeted sensor did not have distinctly better fluorescence performance in terms of signal to noise compared to iGluSnFR.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the relative performance of the sensors.

claim: A recent report used the principle of tethering to localise the signal.
source: A recent report used the principle of tethering to localise the signal (Aggarwal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a reference to recent related work.

claim: One disadvantage of targeting may be that non-synaptic signals of interest could be lost.
source: One disadvantage of targeting may be that non-synaptic signals of interest could be lost.
evidence: This is a logical consideration about the limitations of targeted sensors.

claim: The synaptic localisation does not guarantee to measure exclusively synaptic glutamate.
source: More critically, the synaptic localisation does not guarantee to measure exclusively synaptic glutamate; waves of elevated glutamate from other sources including astroglia, substantial spillover or even changes in the optical properties of tissue could be mistaken for synaptic glutamate in this context, and this is a limitation of our approach.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of signals from targeted sensors.

claim: Spectral variants with distinct (or no) targeting could be combined to get a fuller picture of both synaptic and spillover glutamate.
source: Spectral variants with distinct (or no) targeting could be combined to get a fuller picture of both synaptic and spillover glutamate (see Hao and Plested, 2022 for discussion).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work based on the current findings.

claim: Various approaches are known to augment the signal from iGluSnFR including using the superfolder variant of GFP, mutagenesis, or a different promoter.
source: Various approaches are known to augment the signal from iGluSnFR including using the superfolder variant of GFP (Marvin et al., 2018), mutagenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), or a different promoter (we used human Synapsin).
evidence: This is a summary of known approaches to improve sensor performance.

claim: The superfolder variant of iGluSnFR could be used very successfully for quantal analysis in cell culture, when analysis was confined to axonal projections (i.e., presynaptic sites).
source: Indeed, the superfolder variant of iGluSnFR could be used very successfully for quantal analysis in cell culture, when analysis was confined to axonal projections (i.e., presynaptic sites, Mendonça et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a reference to recent work showing successful quantal analysis with presynaptic iGluSnFR.

claim: Other tethers, either minimal ones or those based on other synaptic proteins, may also give better, more defined, or even orthogonal signals.
source: Finally, other tethers, either minimal ones (Li and Blanpied, 2016) or those based on other synaptic proteins, may also give better, more defined, or even orthogonal signals.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work based on the current findings.
